calibration: The learner can evaluate linear expressions and read Cartesian graphs, but has not learned limits, absolute-value notation, or quantified definitions. They want an introductory interpretation and use of limits and one-sided limits, not a formal analysis course.
review: Keep the small distance convention within its meaningful use. Supply a concrete reasoning bridge, preserve useful work without formalism, and give the later one-sided treatment a distinct ability.

nodes.label: Límite como comportamiento cercano
nodes.explanation: Suponer evaluación de expresiones lineales y lectura de gráficas cartesianas, pero no límites ni valor absoluto. Desarrollar el significado de acercarse a un valor de entrada sin usar necesariamente ese punto, y distinguir el valor de la función del límite. Usar f(x)=2x+1 para x distinto de 2, con un valor en 2 que puede faltar o ser diferente. Explicar |x-2| como distancia y conectar |f(x)-5|=2|x-2| con una exigencia concreta de cercanía; esta notación se introduce dentro de su uso, sin una lección separada. Mostrar qué permite concluir la regla y qué no garantiza una tabla finita por sí sola. Practicar la interpretación de otra regla lineal. Excluir la definición cuantificada formal y las técnicas de cálculo de límites.

nodes.label: Límites laterales
nodes.explanation: A partir del límite como comportamiento cercano, distinguir acercamiento por la izquierda y por la derecha y decidir cuándo ambos permiten un límite bilateral. Introducir la notación lateral y la lectura de una regla por tramos durante un caso accesible, sin suponerlas conocidas. Trabajar con f(x)=x+1 para x<0 y f(x)=2x+3 para x>0; desarrollar los dos valores de acercamiento y por qué su desacuerdo impide un límite bilateral. Practicar con un caso nuevo que cambie si los valores coinciden. Mantener la interpretación informal; excluir demostraciones cuantificadas y clasificación exhaustiva de discontinuidades.

source: In an orthonormal basis |0>, |1>, |2>, prepare (|0>+|1>+|2>)/sqrt(3). Compare two procedures conditioned on the retained report '0 or 1'. Procedure F measures the three rank-one projectors, then hides whether the fine outcome was 0 or 1. Procedure C directly measures the two projectors P01=diag(1,1,0) and P2=diag(0,0,1), with the selective projection prescription. A second measurement tests Q+=|+><+|, |+>=(|0>+|1>)/sqrt(2), with no intervening evolution. Both retained reports have probability 2/3, but the subsequent Q+ probabilities differ: 1/2 for F and 1 for C.
calibration: The learner knows bra-ket notation, normalized pure states, density matrices as mixtures, matrix products, traces, and Born probabilities. They have used rank-one projectors but not subspace projectors, selective updates, or unread measurement ensembles. The target is to follow the stated calculation, accepting the physical update prescriptions.
review: Preserve two independent foundations and both terminal prerequisites. Equal reports must not imply equal operations. Carry the source setup, retained selection and no-evolution assumption into the final brief. Supply the physical prescription explicitly rather than demanding its proof.

tree.topic: Coarse measurement reports and subsequent predictions

nodes.label: Selective and unread projective updates
nodes.explanation: Assume normalized states, density matrices as mixtures, rank-one projectors, traces, matrix multiplication, and Born probabilities. Supply the ideal selective prescription rho_i=P_i rho P_i/Tr(rho P_i) as a physical input. Develop how conditioning selects a normalized branch and how an unread fine result instead gives the probability-weighted mixture, sum_i P_i rho P_i. Explain which operation was carried out and which record was retained. Work a small rank-one example through a later Born prediction, introducing update notation locally. Practice a fresh selection or forgotten-record case. Do not derive the physical prescription or assume that erasing a report reverses its operation.

nodes.label: Projection onto a subspace
nodes.explanation: Assume orthonormal basis states, inner products, matrix products, normalization, and rank-one projectors. Develop P=|0><0|+|1><1| as the projection onto their span in a three-dimensional space. Apply it to an arbitrary vector, identify the components it keeps, and normalize a nonzero projected vector; connect P squared=P to its action. Practice a different subspace or vector. This node teaches the algebra of a subspace projector, including preservation of relative components, not a physical measurement-update law or general spectral theory.

nodes.label: Coarse reports versus coarse operations
nodes.explanation: Use the established selective and unread updates and subspace projection to compare two actual procedures. In orthonormal basis |0>, |1>, |2>, the initial state is (|0>+|1>+|2>)/sqrt(3). F measures the three rank-one projectors, then retains only the report '0 or 1'; C directly measures P01=diag(1,1,0) and P2=diag(0,0,1). Explicitly supply the ideal selective projection prescription for C as a physical input. Develop each state conditioned on the retained report before calculating a second measurement of Q+=|+><+| with |+>=(|0>+|1>)/sqrt(2), assuming no intervening evolution. Show why equal retained-report probabilities of 2/3 coexist with subsequent Q+ probabilities 1/2 for F and 1 for C. Explain the distinction between concealing finer data and performing a coarser operation. Include fresh reasoning with established updates and projectors; exclude general measurement instruments and proofs of the update postulates.

source: Synthetic committee memo: 'Before shorter shifts, inspectors recorded 80 defective items among 1,000 produced; afterward, 60 among 600. The fall proves reduced fatigue improved quality, so extend the policy.' The memo also notes that product mix and inspection procedures changed between periods. It gives no comparison group or adjustment for those changes.
calibration: The learner reads ordinary prose and can divide and multiply, but has not evaluated changing-denominator comparisons or separated an observation from a causal claim. They want to evaluate this memo, not survey industrial history or learn causal inference theory.
review: Keep the actual passage and numbers accessible without the source attachment. Cover both numerical and evidential interpretation; do not import a history course or formal causal model.

nodes.label: Counts and rates with changing totals
nodes.explanation: Assume division, multiplication, and ordinary reading. Develop a rate as a count relative to its relevant total, introducing percentages as per-hundred comparisons when needed. Work a case in which the smaller count accompanies a larger rate and show how equal denominators make comparison possible. Practice deciding which comparison a stated claim needs. Exclude sampling uncertainty, significance tests, and causal attribution.

nodes.label: Observation and causal claims in a memo
nodes.explanation: Assume ordinary prose reading. Distinguish what a short memo reports, what cause it proposes, and what action it recommends. Work a small textual case through those distinctions and explain why a simultaneous change can leave a proposed explanation unsettled. Practice identifying the observation, proposed cause, and missing comparison in another case. Do not introduce formal causal inference or require numerical rate comparisons in this node.

nodes.label: Evaluating the shorter-shifts recommendation
nodes.explanation: Combine changing-total comparisons with the distinction between observation and causal claim to evaluate this synthetic memo: 'Before shorter shifts, inspectors recorded 80 defective items among 1,000 produced; afterward, 60 among 600. The fall proves reduced fatigue improved quality, so extend the policy.' The memo also reports changes in product mix and inspection procedures, with no comparison group or adjustment. Develop the difference between the falling count and the rising defect rate, 8% versus 10%, then assess which parts of the proposed causal explanation and recommendation the available evidence supports. Preserve the uncertainty caused by changed conditions rather than asserting the policy helped or harmed quality. Practice identifying an additional comparison that would address a stated gap. Exclude an industrial-history survey and formal causal models.

source: Synthetic model note: x(t)=v0*t+a*t^2/2, x_approx(t)=v0*t, with v0=4 m/s and a=0.2 m/s^2, constant on 0<=t<=T. Require |x(t)-x_approx(t)|/|x_approx(t)| <= 0.05 for every 0<t<=T. This denominator is the approximation, not the exact displacement. The initial correction vanishes at t=0; that alone does not establish validity on the interval.
calibration: The learner can evaluate expressions, compare positive quantities, rearrange linear inequalities, and interpret units. They have not studied calculus. The displacement law is a supplied model, not a result they are asked to derive.
review: A single coherent node can introduce relative error in its actual use. Keep the model law supplied, identify the correct error denominator, and justify the whole validity interval without calculus or an unrelated approximation course.

tree.topic: Validity interval of a constant-speed displacement approximation

nodes.label: Validity of a constant-speed approximation
nodes.explanation: Assume expression evaluation, positive-quantity comparisons, linear inequalities, and units, but no calculus. Supply x(t)=v0*t+a*t^2/2 and x_approx(t)=v0*t as the model with constant v0=4 m/s and a=0.2 m/s^2 on 0<=t<=T; do not derive these laws. Develop the requirement |x(t)-x_approx(t)|/|x_approx(t)|<=0.05 for every 0<t<=T, explaining absolute value locally as magnitude. The denominator is the approximated displacement, not the exact one. Show the correction ratio a*t/(2*v0), why its largest value on this interval occurs at T, and how this gives T<=2 seconds. Treat t=0 as the shared zero displacement, where the displayed relative ratio is undefined; do not use its vanishing correction as evidence for later validity. Practice comparing candidate intervals or changing a parameter using the same established reasoning. Exclude calculus derivations and other approximation methods.

calibration: The learner knows arithmetic but not quantity-weighted totals, percentage discounts, or accounting for returned items. The destination is simple transaction revenue after one discount and full-price-equivalent returns, with successive discounts as optional enrichment.
review: The app removes transitive edges. The terminal brief must still carry the needed earlier relation and conditions. Optional enrichment must not block the core destination.

nodes.label: Line-item totals
nodes.explanation: Assume arithmetic. Develop a transaction total as sum_i q_i*p_i, explaining quantity q_i and unit price p_i together with their units. Work a mixed-item purchase and practice a new one; distinguish unit price from line total. Exclude discounts and returns.

nodes.label: A percentage discount on a purchase
nodes.explanation: Use established line-item totals to develop a percentage discount as a fraction of the transaction amount. Introduce d as the discount fraction and derive amount_paid=total*(1-d), checking its meaning against a worked purchase. Practice comparing discount offers on different totals. Exclude returns, taxes, and successive discounts.

nodes.label: Net revenue after discounted-item returns
nodes.explanation: Build on the one-discount amount and the earlier relation total=sum_i q_i*p_i for quantities q_i and unit prices p_i. A single discount fraction d applies equally to all items; r_i<=q_i are returned quantities, each refunded at its discounted purchase price, with no fees or taxes. Develop net_revenue=sum_i (q_i-r_i)*p_i*(1-d) by identifying the amount kept from each line and then summing it. Explain why refunding undiscounted prices would change the model. Work a purchase with a partial return and practice diagnosing a proposed refund or comparing two return patterns. Exclude successive discounts and general accounting conventions.

nodes.label: Successive percentage discounts
nodes.explanation: Use a single percentage discount to develop the effect of applying a second discount to the already reduced amount. Derive the retained fraction (1-d1)*(1-d2), compare it with adding discount percentages, and practice a fresh offer comparison. Exclude returns and accounting policy. This is enrichment outside the net-revenue destination.
